title: Two-way tables and relative frequencies
keyIdea: A two-way table counts people by two categories at once, such as year group and favourite activity. Each person sits in exactly one cell; row totals add across, column totals add down, and both sets add to the grand total. A relative frequency is a count divided by a total. Divide by the grand total for a joint relative frequency (Year 9 and music, out of everyone). Divide by a row or column total for a conditional one (music, out of the Year 9s). Two variables are associated when the conditional relative frequencies differ between rows; compare percentages, not counts, because groups differ in size.
familyTip: Ask everyone at a family gathering two questions, like adult or child and tea or juice, and build the table together on paper. Then ask: what fraction of the children chose juice? And what fraction of everyone are children who chose juice? Talk about why the answers differ.

visual.caption: What do you divide by? Drag each question, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort survey cards into a two-way table, fill gaps from totals, tap the right denominator, drag rows to remove an association, judge links.

kid: A two-way table sorts people by two things at once. The rows might be year groups and the columns what they chose. Every person goes in exactly one cell.
Row totals add across. Column totals add down. Both lead to the same grand total, so you can use totals to find a missing cell by subtracting.
A relative frequency is a count divided by a total. Out of everyone, divide by the grand total. Out of one group, such as the Year 9s, divide by that group's total.
To spot a link, compare percentages in each row. If 40% of Year 7s and 40% of Year 9s choose music, there is no link, even if more Year 9s were asked.
adult: Ages 13 to 15. Common Core 8.SP.4 asks students to build and read two-way tables of two categorical variables and to use row or column relative frequencies to describe a possible association. S-ID.5 names joint, marginal and conditional relative frequencies. GCSE Mathematics (AQA 8300, P and S strands) uses two-way tables for frequencies and probabilities.

A joint relative frequency divides a cell by the grand total. A marginal one divides a row or column total by the grand total. A conditional one divides a cell by its row or column total, and the wording tells you which: 'of the Year 9s' means the Year 9 row. Row and column percentages answer different questions, so 30/50 (Year 9s who like music) is not the same as 30/42 (music fans who are Year 9).

Common mistakes: dividing by the grand total when the question names a group, using the row total when the column is meant, adding a cell to a total instead of subtracting, judging association from raw counts when group sizes differ, and reading an association as a cause. Equal conditional relative frequencies in every row mean no association in that sample.

In the lab students sort eight survey cards into a 2 by 2 table, find four missing values from totals in an 80-student table, tap the total to divide by for four questions, drag the Year 9 music count until both rows show 40% (20 of 50), and judge three tables by row percentages.

practice.prompt: Year 7 row: sport 18, music ?, total 30. What is the missing cell?
practice.hint: The two cells in a row add up to the row total.
practice.explain: 18 + ? = 30, so ? = 30 − 18 = 12. Adding 18 to 30 counts the sport fans twice.

practice.prompt: A row total is {t}. One cell in that row is {a}. What is the other cell?
practice.hint: The two cells add to the row total, so subtract the cell you know.

practice.prompt: 80 students: 30 are Year 9s who like music, and there are 50 Year 9s. What fraction of Year 9s like music?
practice.hint: 'Of Year 9s' tells you which total goes on the bottom.
practice.explain: Out of the 50 Year 9s, 30 like music: 30/50 = 0.6. 30/80 is the joint relative frequency, and 50/80 is the share who are in Year 9.

practice.prompt: Of 50 Year 8s, {a} cycle to school. What percentage of the Year 8s cycle?
practice.hint: Divide by the Year 8 total, then multiply by 100.
practice.explain: {a} ÷ 50 × 100 = {=a*2}%. This is a conditional relative frequency: out of the Year 8s only.

practice.prompt: Of 20 left-handers, 6 wear glasses. Of 80 right-handers, 24 wear glasses. Is wearing glasses associated with handedness here?
practice.hint: Turn each row into a percentage before you compare.
practice.explain: 6/20 = 30% and 24/80 = 30%. The counts differ only because the groups differ in size, so there is no association.

pool.prompt: In a survey of 80, 18 are Year 7s who prefer sport. What is the joint relative frequency of Year 7 and sport?
pool.explain: Joint relative frequency divides by the grand total: 18/80 = 0.225. 18/30 is conditional on Year 7, and 18/38 is conditional on sport.

pool.prompt: The two column totals of a two-way table are {a} and {b}. What is the grand total?
pool.hint: Every person is in exactly one column.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. The row totals must add to the same number.

pool.prompt: 42 students prefer music; 30 of them are in Year 9. What fraction of music fans are in Year 9?
pool.hint: 'Of music fans' tells you to divide by the music column total.
pool.explain: Out of the 42 music fans, 30 are Year 9: 30/42 ≈ 0.71. 30/50 answers a different question: the share of Year 9s who like music.

pool.prompt: Of 25 Year 10s asked, {a} have a part-time job. What percentage of these Year 10s have a job?
pool.explain: {a} ÷ 25 × 100 = {=a*4}%. The bottom of the fraction is the Year 10 total, because the question is about Year 10s.

pool.prompt: 70% of dog owners walk daily but only 20% of non-owners do. What can you conclude?
choices: Dog ownership and walking daily are associated
Owning a dog makes people walk
pool.hint: A table shows whether percentages differ. Does it show why?
pool.explain: 70% and 20% differ, so the two are associated. The table cannot show cause: people who already walk may choose to get dogs.

pool.prompt: 40% of the 30 Year 7s and 40% of the 50 Year 9s prefer music. Is year group associated with preferring music?
choices: Yes, the groups are different sizes
pool.hint: Compare the percentages, not the counts.
pool.explain: Both rows are 40%, so there is no association. 20 Year 9s is more than 12 Year 7s only because more Year 9s were asked.

pool.prompt: Year 9 row: sport ?, music 30, total 50. Sport column total is 38. Which is the missing cell?
pool.hint: Use the row: the two Year 9 cells add to 50.
pool.explain: 50 − 30 = 20. Check with the column: Year 7 sport is 38 − 20 = 18. 68 adds instead of subtracting.

pool.prompt: Why do row percentages and column percentages give different answers?
choices: One of them is always wrong
pool.hint: Look at what goes on the bottom of each fraction.
pool.explain: Row percentages divide by a row total and column percentages by a column total, so they answer different questions about the same cell.
